Sarah — thanks for the clear asks and diagram. Below is a concise recommendation you can hand to your auditors; I also attached a short technical proposal (tls-termination-proposal.pdf) and example CSR snippets (csr-examples.txt) for your ops team.

Summary (minimal-risk, customer-managed CA)
- TLS termination location: customer-managed TLS termination at the VPC ingress (private NLB or edge proxy inside the VPC). Redwood runs an internal agent/proxy inside the private runtime that terminates on the customer-provided certificate. This ensures private key material never leaves Northbridge.
- Certificate ownership: Customer generates CSRs and provides signed certs (wildcard or explicit SANs). Redwood accepts PEM/PKCS#7 artifacts during onboarding.
- Trust model: Redwood trusts the customer's CA chain; we require a certificate chain and the intermediate bundle. We do not enroll the cert into Redwood-managed public CAs in this model.
- OCSP/CRL: For long-lived connections, we recommend the customer host an OCSP stapling endpoint close to the ingress (or enable stapling on the NLB) to avoid outbound lookups from Redwood sidecars. Redwood sidecars will respect stapled responses and otherwise perform OCSP with a short timeout.
- SNI/mTLS expectations: For standard TLS (1.2/1.3) we expect SNI to contain the tenant FQDN (no tenant ID substitution). For mTLS flows we support client cert validation against a customer-provided trust root; in those cases the client hello will include SNI = tenant FQDN and the client cert will carry the identity (CN/SAN) used for mapping.

Fallback (Redwood-managed certs)
- TLS termination location: Redwood edge proxy (in Redwood-managed overlay) terminating with Redwood-issued certs. Recommended when customers do not want private key custody.
- Certificate lifecycle: Redwood rotates certs and exposes key metadata via the console. We will publish rotation windows and a notice period.
- Privacy: Customer traffic traverses an encrypted tunnel; Redwood-managed certs mean keys are in Redwood KMS. For regulated customers we recommend the customer-managed model unless an explicit contract clause allows Redwood key custody.

Operational notes and checklist (attached):
- CSR example flavors (SAN vs wildcard), key size/algorithms, and requested TTL.
- NLB Listener / Proxy settings: suggest TLS 1.3 preferred, TLS 1.2 allowed for legacy (disable RC4/1.0/1.1).
- Health checks: use an HTTPS health path that validates only liveness; avoid returning cert chains in health responses.

If this covers the auditors' questions, say so and we'll convert to a signed one-page attestation. If you'd like a short diagram annotated with which components see plaintext (none) vs encrypted (inside VPC only) we can produce that.

Thanks — attaching the proposal now.

Adding a couple implementation caveats from the runtime side:
- SNI routing: If customers present multiple SANs on the same cert we need a deterministic SNI->tenant mapping during the initial handshake. We prefer a primary FQDN be included in onboarding metadata to avoid ambiguous matches.
- OCSP caching: Redwood sidecars maintain a small in-memory OCSP cache for stapled responses; recommend customer configure short TTLs from their OCSP responder but still allow stapling.
- Long-term sessions (LLM streaming): For very long streaming connections we prefer client-side keepalives and periodic OCSP revalidation windows (e.g., every 12h) so we can detect revocations. We do not hold open internal connections indefinitely without periodic revalidation.
- Fallback routing: If SNI is absent or encrypted (ECH) and routing fails, the default behavior is to reject the connection. We can support an allowlist that routes by TCP port in exceptional agreements.

I'll update the proposal PDF with the SNI mapping recommendation and a short table of runtime behaviors.
